transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-09
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Li (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Hearthline Head of Infra), Leah Ortiz (Security), Samir Khan (Platform)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on private/VPC deployment feasibility: cidr/peering, private endpoints, egress and region gating. Customer has strict egress IP controls, SOC2+ finance regs, and wants deterministic latency for inference. Redwood AE + SE explained high-level modes (hosted/dedicated/private) and dug into private onramp patterns and fallbacks.

Topics: private endpoints, transit gateway vs peering, NAT/egress IP requirements, KMS/integration, audit logs, regional availability

[00:00] Jordan Li: Hey all, thanks for joining, uh just to kick off, I'm Jordan with Redwood, Priya's our SE. Could you each do a one-line on expectations?
[00:12] Carlos Mendes: Sure, Carlos here. We're evaluating options for running model inference for our trading signals, mostly private deployment, can't send data to public internet, and we need stable egress IPs for vendor allowlists.
[00:24] Leah Ortiz: Leah, security. We'll need SOC2 in the loop, KMS integration, and probably on-prem/HSM discussion later. Today we're focused on networking and region constraints.
[00:35] Samir Khan: Samir, platform. Primary ask is how Redwood lands in our VPC, whether it's peering, privatelink-like endpoints, or transit gateway. Also curious about cross-region fallbacks.
[00:47] Priya Nair: Great, thanks. High-level: Redwood offers three modes — hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, and private (VPC/on-prem). For private we can either install a private control plane talking over a managed agent, or set up private endpoints into Redwood's infra depending on your preference. We'll walk patterns and tradeoffs.
[01:12] Carlos Mendes: When you say private endpoints, is that equivalent to AWS PrivateLink or something we host? We need an option that doesn't traverse internet egress, like direct interface endpoints.
[01:25] Priya Nair: Yeah, PrivateLink-style interface endpoints are a common pattern. We also support transit gateway peering where you peer via TGW, depending on scale. PrivateLink gives per-region interface endpoints you control. TGW can simplify multi-account, multi-region connectivity but has a little more operational overhead.
[01:45] Leah Ortiz: For us CIDR is strict. We can't accept overlapping ranges; we also need to freeze egress IPs so downstream providers can firewall allow them. Does Redwood publish static egress IPs in private mode?
[01:58] Jordan Li: Short answer: yes, in Private we can provision egress through NATs in your VPC or via a proxied egress with predictable IPs — depends on deployment topology. If Redwood is self-hosted in your VPC (Private with customer-managed dataplane), egress is yours. If Redwood hosts the dataplane but peers privately, we can allocate predictable egress ranges that you allowlist; we'll need to map that to your network plan.
[02:25] Samir Khan: Can you run that back — so in the redwood-hosted private datacenter setup, traffic still leaves to Redwood's infra and comes back? I'm trying to picture the data plane flows.
[02:38] Priya Nair: Sure. There are broadly two patterns: 1) Customer-managed dataplane: we give you an appliance/container that runs in your VPC or on-prem. That means all inference runs inside your network; Redwood control plane is still out-of-band but doesn't see payloads. 2) Redwood-managed private endpoints: Redwood runs inference on our infra but we expose interface endpoints into your VPC — requests go via the interface endpoint to Redwood's private network. In pattern 2, egress for outbound calls from the model (e.g., to an external tool you call) can be routed via our egress or via your configurable NAT — need alignment.
[03:15] Carlos Mendes: Hmm. For compliance we prefer customer-managed dataplane if possible. Do you have an on-prem, air-gapped option?
[03:23] Priya Nair: Yes — we offer an on-prem package for regulated workloads. It can be deployed in an air-gapped cluster; that is a heavier engagement but doable. For many finance customers, customer-managed dataplane in their cloud VPC works well and meets SOC2 if keys and logs are properly integrated.
[03:42] Leah Ortiz: About KMS — can we bring our own key for model encryption and logs? We need KMS/HSM integration and key rotation policies.
[03:52] Jordan Li: Bring-your-own-keys is supported. For Private we can integrate with your KMS (AWS KMS) and for on-prem we can work with an HSM. We'll capture exact integration flows in the security docs.
[04:05] Samir Khan: Regions — we operate in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. We need inference pins in us-east-1 only for latency-sensitive workloads, and eu-west for EU customer data. Do you support regional isolation so traffic never leaves region?
[04:20] Priya Nair: Yes, you can pin model versions to regionally deployed dataplanes. For the private endpoints option, we provision per-region endpoints. For cross-region fallback, there's a routing policy that can failover to another region, but if you require strict regional residency, you can disable cross-region fallbacks.
[04:43] Carlos Mendes: What about peering limits — our security team wants to avoid lots of VPC peering connections. Is TGW recommended?
[04:53] Priya Nair: For many multi-account setups TGW simplifies it. PrivateLink is per-region and per-account unless you use a central transit in front. We usually recommend TGW where you have many spoke accounts. There's also an option to front a centralized NAT/proxy that handles egress allowlisting.
[05:12] Leah Ortiz: Audit logs — we need per-request audit logs forwarded to our SIEM with request IDs stripped of PII, retention for 7 years, and immutable storage. Can Redwood forward logs to our S3 or to a logging endpoint?
[05:26] Jordan Li: Yes, Redwood can push audit logs to your S3 bucket or to a logging collector over private connectivity. We also have built-in RBAC and token-level attribution shown in Redwood Console. For PII redaction we can integrate post-processing in the log pipeline. We'll need to validate legal retention and encryption in transit and at rest.
[05:47] Samir Khan: Bandwidth/throughput question — our inference patterns are spiky at market open. How does autoscaling work with a private dataplane, and how do you handle burst capacity?
[05:59] Priya Nair: Autoscaling for Dedicated and Private has two axes: vertical (bigger GPUs) and horizontal (more replicas). In customer-managed dataplane you control autoscaling using our operator; we provide metrics and recommended scaling policies. For Redwood-managed private pools we can allocate burst capacity with reserved burst nodes in your region to keep latency SLOs. There's also continuous batching which improves throughput.
[06:28] Carlos Mendes: Any limits on KV cache sharing or multi-tenant isolation that might affect latency?
[06:35] Priya Nair: KV cache is per-model instance; in dedicated/private we can provision isolated caches per-customer to avoid noisy neighbor interference. For hosted multi-tenant we do soft isolation which is fine for non-prod.
[06:48] Leah Ortiz: On the networking split: who maintains route tables and security groups in the PrivateLink pattern?
[06:56] Priya Nair: The customer manages route tables and SGs in their VPC; Redwood provides the interface endpoint configuration. For TGW we coordinate attachments and route announcements. We'll provide an ops checklist so your cloud network team knows what to add.
[07:12] Jordan Li: Quick practical question — do you have an existing transit gateway or are you using peering today?
[07:18] Samir Khan: Today it's peering between a couple accounts; we've not fully adopted TGW yet. Might be a spot to simplify.
[07:25] Jordan Li: Ok, TGW might be cleaner as you scale. We'll send a mapping doc.
[07:30] Priya Nair: Also note egress NAT gateway costs — if you require fixed egress IPs we can propose either static NAT or use a central egress proxy that you manage. That will affect cost.
[07:44] Carlos Mendes: Cost is a consideration — predictable egress + private endpoints adds network bill. We'll weigh that against risk.
[07:51] Leah Ortiz: Another item: penetration testing. We need to include Redwood in our annual pentest scope and get vendor questionnaires. Can you ship SOC2/ISO certs and a pen-test window?
[08:02] Jordan Li: Yes, we'll share our compliance pack. For customer-managed dataplane pen-testing is on your side; for Redwood-managed components we'll coordinate.
[08:12] Samir Khan: Benchmarks — we want a latency run for our 512-token prompts in us-east-1 with p95 < 120ms. Can you run a small benchmark or share prior numbers?
[08:23] Priya Nair: We'll do an SE deep-dive to run benchmarks with your prompt set. In dedicated/private we can tune kernel selection and batching to hit p95 targets. We'll need a sample prompt suite and expected concurrency to simulate.
[08:39] Carlos Mendes: About ingress — we prefer TLS mutual auth into the endpoint for additional assurance. Does Redwood support mTLS?
[08:48] Priya Nair: We do support client cert-based auth for private endpoints; we can layer that with token auth. We'll include that in the config examples.
[08:58] Leah Ortiz: And SSO — we use Okta. We need SAML-based SSO and SCIM for user provisioning.
[09:06] Jordan Li: Redwood supports SAML/Okta and SCIM provisioning for the console. For API keys we can tie tokens to user accounts with RBAC.
[09:16] Samir Khan: Any special network ACLs or IP fragmentation gotchas for high-throughput UDP? Our infra sometimes uses UDP but inference is TCP, so probably fine.
[09:26] Priya Nair: Inference uses TCP and websockets for streaming. No special UDP needs. Recommend MTU tests but nothing out of the ordinary.
[09:36] Jordan Li: Let's capture immediate blockers — sounds like CIDR allocation, egress allowlist, and SOC2/pen-test are the big ones. Anything else?
[09:45] Leah Ortiz: Data residency confirmation for eu-west-1 workloads — we need an attestation that logs and model cache won't cross region.
[09:53] Priya Nair: We'll document regional isolation guarantees and describe how we pin caches/models. If you pick strict residency we disable cross-region failover.
[10:05] Carlos Mendes: One more on maintenance windows and upgrades — we need a predictable upgrade process. How are rollouts handled in Private?
[10:12] Priya Nair: We support canary rollouts and you can pin to a model version. For customer-managed dataplane upgrades are scheduled with your ops team; for Redwood-managed private we do staged rollouts and have automatic fallback policies.
[10:26] Jordan Li: Ok that's a good list. Next steps: we'll send the private deployment network diagram, a sample terraform for interface endpoints, and a short doc on burst capacity. Priya will run a follow-up benchmark session when you share prompts.
[10:42] Samir Khan: Great. In terms of timeline, we aim to start a pilot in January with a two-week POC. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[10:51] Jordan Li: No major blockers. We'll need your CIDRs and auth patterns, plus security questionnaires filled. We'll aim to get the security pack to you by end of week.
[11:02] Leah Ortiz: We'll circulate the vendor questionnaire after this call.
[11:08] Jordan Li: Perfect. Anything else before we close?
[11:12] Carlos Mendes: Nope, thanks — appreciate the clear patterns.
[11:15] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the deck and ops checklist.
[11:20] End of call

Notes about transcript quality: audio was clear but some product names and acronyms were auto-corrected, e.g., "PrivateLink" transcribed as "private link", "KV cache" sometimes as "K V cache", a few timestamps slightly off.
